newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK mulls relaxing some leveraged forex regulations.
newsitem.headline: HK mulls relaxing some leveraged forex regulations.

text.p: Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) issued for consultation on Wednesday a paper recommending relaxation of some of the rules and regulations imposed on leveraged foreign exchange trading.
- The minimum liquid capital requirement of HK$25 million for licensed traders be reduced to HK$15 million with a view to further reductions if necessary
- The maximum aggregate gross position of 60 times liquid capital to cap traders' risk-taking ability be retained

- The SFC be empowered to amend the minimum margin requirements for specific institutions which have introduced a "no over-loss rule" into their standard client agreements and can demonstrate they can ensure compliance with the rule.
- The SFC be empowered to waive the current requirement banning licensed traders from extending credit for margin deposits of high net worth clients

- The rules for segregated trust accounts be relaxed to enable traders to lay off client positions with SFC-approved instititions using money on deposit with traders, provided the current protections already afforded clients are preserved
- Licensed traders be required to take out fidelity insurance commensurate with liabilities.

- The review, however, recommended that initial capital requirements of HK$30 million in paid-in capital for licensed traders be retained as a barrier to "fly-by-night traders and to ensure that traders are adequately capitalised."
Hong Kong implemented laws to regulate leveraged foreign exchange trading in September 1994 after a series of fraud and malpractice cases.
The regulators are seeking comment on the latest review which concluded the regulations had brought "a much-needed measure of discipline to the industry as well as greater protection to investors."
But it also noted the industry has experienced a "significant contraction, both in terms of business volume and in the number of firms" in the 18 months since the regulations were implemented.

It suggested this was a result of the impact of the regulations, particularly the increased margin and minimum capital requirements, a migration of businesses to Macau, a ban by mainland Chinese authorities of leveraged forex trading and increased competition from large retail banks.
The deadline for submissions is September 30, 1996.
